newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota says no decision made on European plant.
newsitem.headline: Toyota says no decision made on European plant.

text.p: Japan's car giant Toyota Motor Co on Monday said while it was considering additional investment in Europe, it was still weighing its options over which country to invest in, and by how much.

Britain's Financial Times reported on Monday that Toyota is considering France as the location for its second European production plant. It said Toyota is considering building a $1.6 billion car plant in Lens in northern France in an attempt to raise its European sales by 50 percent by the year 2000.
A Toyota official denied the report, saying that the company was still studying many possible options for its European investment.
"We have no such plans and have not decided anything about future investment in Europe. It is now under study, including whether we need an additional new plant in Europe," a Toyota spokesman said.
Industry analysts said that while Toyota would prefer to invest in continental Europe rather than in Britain, they were not certain if the carmaker will choose France as the venue.

"It's up to what type of model Toyota wants to produce. (A plant in Lens) is possible if Toyota wants to make the profitable medium-class or larger car. If it wants to produce compact cars, Eastern Europe is better," Nomura Research analyst Seiji Sugiura said.
Other analysts were more sceptical about any fresh investment in France by Toyota, mainly in view of the production costs.

"Logically, the possibility of a Toyota plant in France is very weak. Eastern Europe is better in view of low production costs, parts sourcing and a potentially sharp growth in the car market there," said Koji Endo, a senior vice president of Lehman Brothers Japan.

Toyota Motor president Hiroshi Okuda stirred up controversy in Britain last month by saying that Toyota would rather put new investment into continental Europe if Britain stayed out of Europe's single currency.

Okuda later issued an official statement, saying that in general a unified currency would limit currency risks and would be a significant advantage. He said future investment in Britain was being considered as one of many possible options.
Toyota has said it plans to increase its 1997 sales in Europe by more than nine percent from a year earlier to 450,000 cars, and by nearly 50 percent to 600,000 cars by the beginning of next century.
Toyota is now building its second factory in Derbyshire, England, to boost the production capacity of Toyota Motor Manufacturing (UK) Ltd to a total 200,000 cars by late 1998, up from 100,000 now.
Toyota also has a Turkish car plant where it produces 26,000 vehicles in 1996.
